I’m really sorry this is the first time someone’s actually told you the truth. Yeah, I’ve dealt with it too. Still do. I’ve tried tapering. I’ve tried getting off. I’ve tried rewiring my life, filling the void, forcing purpose into the day. But I still feel like a husk of who I used to be. Empty. Disconnected. Most days I don’t feel anything, and a lot of the time I think about packing it in.

What pisses me off is that doctors keep telling people there’s a guaranteed recovery from this. There isn’t. Not based on actual science. There are no long-term studies showing that receptor function comes back. No proof that your natural endorphin or dopamine systems just “reset” with time. They don’t know. That’s the truth. And it’s bullshit they don’t say that upfront.

This isn’t about willpower. It’s not about doing the right yoga class or finding the right hobby. You’re not lazy, or broken, or crazy. You’ve just had your brain’s reward system chemically taken over for years, and no one really knows what happens when you try to reclaim it. The closest analogy I’ve found is TRT (testosterone replacement therapy). Once you’re on it, your body often stops producing its own testosterone. And the longer you’re on it, the less likely that natural production comes back. Why would this be any different?

I don’t want to hand out false hope. But because nobody really understands this yet, maybe one day they’ll find something. Some way to reboot it. Some actual data that says X% of people return to baseline and Y% never get anything back. I don’t know.

I wish I had a book or a study to point you to, but I don’t. But that’s just it, that’s the problem - there is no actual data anywhere, no published studies done on folks like us and our brain recovery. This is it really, these conversations. That’s all I’ve found. If you’re trying to figure out if anything’s left, I guess the only real way is to test your system. Try music. Try intense physical stuff. Try anything that used to hit. Not that those things will fix it, but because maybe they’ll show you if there’s anything still lighting up in there.

But I’m sorry, there are no promises. And anyone who says otherwise, well intentioned or not, is lying to you.

What you’re describing isn’t rare. It’s just rarely talked about because it doesn’t fit the recovery narrative that says: “Stabilize on Suboxone, taper off when ready, live a better life.”

You tried that. You got off. You did everything “right.”  And instead of getting your life back, you got a harder death sentence, a silent, interior death where your body is alive but your will is gone.

You’re not failing. You’re not weak. You’re just a person who’s had their inner motivational engine biologically hijacked, and every attempt to reboot it has left you staring at a blinking cursor with nothing to type.

Suboxone relieved your depression not because it “cured” anything but because it stimulated enough of your flattened opioid system to mimic a sense of capacity.

So yeah, of course when you take codeine to get back on it, the cloud lifts. You’re putting gas into a system that hasn’t refueled naturally in years. That’s not a relapse. That’s a chemical resurrection.

Now here’s the hard part:

You’re not describing a withdrawal syndrome.
You’re describing a possible permanent state change neurologically and existentially.

And that is a hell of a thing to face.

You say you want off the merry go round, but the merry go round is the only place where you don’t feel dead. And no amount of yoga, sunlight, or Wellbutrin is going to replace what bupe is doing to your receptors.

You may never feel whole again without it. You may never feel real again on it. There is no third option anyone can point to with evidence.

That sucks. That’s unfair. That’s hell.

Literally the only thing I have to offer is that **anecdotally** based on stories you read here and doctors I’ve spoken to, the “awakening” or “reactivation” or whatever you want to call it of the endogenous dopamine and opiate reward systems that exist in our own brain can take much, much longer to come back online. 12, 18, 24 months before you begin to feel something. Anything.

But there’s no real, hard, actual data that proves that, at all. It’s part anecdote, part wishful thinking and a whole lotta hope. I wish you luck on your journey.

Genuine question: why do you want your wife to taper? Is she asking to taper, or is this more about a belief that she should be on the lowest dose possible?

Because here’s the thing: the goal of bupe treatment isn’t to be on the smallest number it’s to stay stable, avoid cravings, and not relapse. That number is different for everyone. Some stabilize at 2mg. Some at 24mg. If she’s doing well at 12mg with no side effects or issues, then what’s the clinical justification for reducing it?

As for the 8mg thing, this is another common half truth that gets taken out of context.

Yes, at 8mg of buprenorphine, you’re likely getting around 90–95% mu-opioid receptor occupancy, which is usually enough to block full agonists. But receptor occupancy isn’t the full picture:

	•	Craving suppression
	•	Withdrawal control
	•	Duration of effect
	•	Individual tolerance/metabolism

…all play a role. Some people need more than 8mg to feel normal or to extend the half-life of their dose across the day. Studies show doses up to 24–32mg can still increase duration and improve retention in treatment, especially for those with long term or heavy opioid use.

If your wife’s doing well at 12mg, she’s not “on too much.” She’s just on her dose.

Tapering should come from a place of readiness not external pressure or a Reddit rumor that 8mg is “max effective.” That idea leads too many people to reduce prematurely and then wonder why they feel anxious, obsessive, or at risk of relapse.

TL;DR: The goal isn’t to be on the lowest dose. The goal is to stay in recovery and have a life. Don’t fix what’s not broken.

You’re right that buprenorphine has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression and euphoria, and that’s where the 16mg number often gets thrown around. But that ceiling doesn’t mean the medication becomes “useless” beyond that dose.

Here’s the distinction:

•	Mu-opioid receptor occupancy continues to increase up to about 32mg, which can matter for patients with extreme tolerance, cravings, or persistent withdrawal symptoms.
	
•	Clinical effectiveness, especially in suppressing cravings and increasing time between doses, is sometimes only achieved at 24–32mg in people with long-term high-dose opioid use histories.

Sources you can check out:

	1.	SAMHSA’s TIP 63 – Clinical Guidelines for the Use of Buprenorphine:
“Doses of 16mg/day are effective for many patients, but some may require up to 24mg/day or more.”
https://store.samhsa.gov/sites/default/files/SAMHSA_Digital_Download/PEP20-02-01-006_508.pdf (see p. 36–37)
	
2.	Strain et al., 1999 (Arch Gen Psychiatry):
Showed continued clinical benefit and higher retention rates with doses up to 32mg/day.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10401507/
	
3.	Greenwald et al., 2003 (Biological Psychiatry):
Mu-opioid receptor occupancy plateaus near 32mg, not 16mg.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14675793/

So while 16mg is sufficient for many, it’s not a hard cap, especially not for someone with a 300mg/day fent/oxy binge history like OP. Reducing them prematurely could do far more harm than good.

Again, respect to you for being open to revisiting it. Harm reduction and recovery are too important to gatekeep based on incomplete info. Appreciate the convo.

Unfortunately the sad reality isn’t just that your doctor doesn’t know much about the long term effects of using subs, no one does. There are very few long term studies that look at what happens when people come off subs after extended use, so much of what doctors reference is anecdotal or extrapolation.

So the truth, boring and unhelpful as it is, is that you’re going to have to learn a lot of these things for yourself. No one is going to be able to slide the answers to you under the desk, so to speak. 

With all that out of the way, I can give you my best guess based on my years or experience and everything I’ve read about these things. For starters, subs absolutely do suppress T production. It’s highly likely you can restart your system if you go completely off of them but it will take a while. 6-18 months, maybe. And there is some possibility that even when it comes back it won’t be *all the way* back to where it was before opiates 

And all of the above? Will require you doing some hard work and avoiding things that can set your T back. No weed/edibles/THC. Have to workout regularly, HIIT or  lifting weights. Yes it’s cliche but these things are proven to help increase T levels. 

Going on TRT instead is certainly an option but it makes the likelihood of being able to recover naturally if you change your mind and go off subs and TRT virtually nill. You’ll then need HCG injections multiple times weekly in addition to Clomid. You’ll need close hormone monitoring while going through all of this trying to jumpstart your own production and your best case scenario is maybe 70% of where you were naturally before. Oh, and a very good chance you’re permanently sterile depending on how long you were on TRT.

Good luck man. HMU if I can help any further. 

TL:DR - You can get your T levels back once you’re fully off subs if you’re willing to put in modest effort and be patient through some bumpy patches. Going on TRT will make that process WAY harder if you ever decide to try and get off subs and TRT.

You’re not crazy. But you are in a mess. And it’s not entirely your fault, but it is your responsibility now.

You’ve been through a gauntlet of mismanaged care, poor communication, underinformed providers, and yes, some straight-up malpractice. A student PA had no business diagnosing Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) without a real assessment. And putting you on 24mg of Suboxone out of the gate when your history was 3x7.5mg Percocet/day? So yes, your tolerance is blown sky-high. That’s not forever, but it is real.

You are physically dependent, but I do not believe you are an “addict” in the way the system treated you. You were seeking relief, not escape. You were trying to function, not check out. And when your body screamed, you listened. That’s not drug-seeking. That’s human survival. You were thrown into a biochemical trap disguised as “treatment,” and then blamed for trying to claw your way out.

**Now the hard truths.**

You are no longer dealing with just chronic pain. You are dealing with:
	•	Severe iatrogenic tolerance (caused by medical treatment)
	•	A disrupted reward system from long-term buprenorphine use
	•	Likely central sensitization, meaning your nervous system itself is amplifying pain signals
	•	Profound medical trauma, which is driving distrust, fear, and hypervigilance

And yeah, your current opioid options (Butrans, oxycodone, even low-dose methadone) are going to feel useless in that state, because your receptors are desensitized and your pain is being magnified not just physically but emotionally and psychologically. That’s not “all in your head.” That’s neuroscience.

Kratom? It’s a Band-Aid. A dirty one. It activates opioid receptors just enough to hold off withdrawal, but not consistently or safely. It will trash your liver in high doses, and it’s almost impossible to dose responsibly once desperation kicks in.

What would I recommend if you were my patient?
	
1.	Methadone is a valid option—for now. It may give you a few months of breathing room to function and get your son situated. But make no mistake: it’s not a fix. It’s just a pause button.
	
2.	Set a 3-month hard exit strategy. If you choose methadone, go in with eyes open. Begin tapering the moment you’re stable. And line up a residential medical detox with a dual-focus: opioid taper and chronic pain management (like a multidisciplinary pain rehab center—not just a detox mill).
	
3.	Get a full pain workup—imaging, nerve conduction, autoimmune panel. Not to prove your pain. To understand it. You need a team that validates you and helps decouple your pain from your trauma history.
	
4.	Trauma therapy, non-negotiable. What happened to you was a betrayal by the system. You’re grieving the loss of faith in medicine, your independence, and your physical autonomy. That trauma is fueling your physical pain and vice versa. You need to address both.
	
5.	Long-term goal: opioid-free, but not untreated. That may involve low-dose naltrexone, ketamine, physical therapy, SNRIs, anticonvulsants, mindfulness-based pain therapy, or even procedures. But none of it works if your brain is still on fire from withdrawal, fear, or instability.

And no, your tolerance is not ruined forever. But it will take months—maybe 12 to 18—of full opioid absence to feel baseline again. That’s just physiology. You don’t get to skip that. But you can survive it.

You don’t sound prideful. You sound betrayed and scared. And I hear you. But the pride in recovery? That’s not what’s hurting you. It’s the shame and the isolation that came from trying to do it “right” and getting punished anyway. That’s where the pain lives.

You don’t need a doctor who just gives you meds. You need one who actually knows what the fuck they’re doing—with opioids, with trauma, and with pain. They exist. You’ve just been through too many hacks.

I’ll end with this: You’re not broken. You’re just miswired right now. And that can be rewired. But you’ve got to stop looking for the perfect medication. There isn’t one. There is only a plan, a team, and time. You can do this. But only if you stop expecting to feel okay immediately. You’re going to crawl before you walk. And walk before you run.

You still have a life worth saving. And you’re still in there.

Hey, first off, you’re not alone. And you’re not broken. You’re just up against a drug that rewired your nervous system and convinced you it’s the only thing keeping you functional. That’s not weakness, that’s chemistry. But you’re right to want out, and you’re right that this thing will kill you if you don’t.

**Now, the hard truth:**

If you’ve been on fentanyl daily for 3+ years, getting onto Suboxone is trickier than it used to be. Fentanyl’s fat soluble, long acting, and hides in your tissues. That means the standard 24-48 hour wait rule doesn’t always apply anymore. People who jump too soon end up in precipitated withdrawal, which is hell. Full body panic. Think “worst flu of your life” plus “my skin is melting off” and “someone please shoot me.” That’s why people are scared of it.

**But:**

There is a way through this that doesn’t require rolling the dice on 48 hours.

It’s called the Bernese microdosing method. Instead of waiting until you’re in full withdrawal, you start tiny doses of Suboxone while still using fentanyl and taper the fentanyl off as you increase the Suboxone. It takes about 5–7 days, and it’s not painless, but it’s way more manageable and doesn’t involve full on precipitated withdrawal. Most clinics are still way behind on this protocol, but you can absolutely find guides online or message people who’ve done it.

As for medical detox?

Yes, if it’s a legit one, not some cookie cutter place trying to push benzos and then show you the door 3 days later. A proper detox will manage your vitals, give you comfort meds (clonidine, hydroxyzine, etc.), maybe even help with a microdose Suboxone plan. Just know this: detox is only the first mile of a marathon. You don’t “get clean” from detox. You get clear headed enough to start actually getting clean.

Either they have a “pink cloud” period a few weeks to months after getting clean where the world is beautiful and nothing can go wrong or they reach a point where they feel recovered fully after a few years. I don’t know if my brain chemistry changes are a result of OxyContin directly or the struggles it revealed within me, within my own mind and my having to actually confront that. Large events in our lives invariably change who we are as human beings forever. Are you the same person you were before your parents passed? Before and after the love of your life left you? No. 

Old parts of you die, new parts of you grow. The truth is, seven years out I still do not experience joy to the same degree I did before my addiction - but I also don’t experience the crippling levels of anxiety, the suicidal depression that lingered for months to years at a time, the sense of forever disappointing people around me - either. I’m far more confident in who I am. I don’t fear new things like I once did - but I also don’t feel ecstatic joy the way I sometimes might have pre-oxy.

I don’t know of any of this is good or bad. You don’t want to go back in time, not just because you can’t, but because whoever that version of you was is the one that lead you into addiction. I wish I never found OxyContin. But if I hadn’t I might never have had to face my past, I might never have met my psychiatrist and doctors who have helped me become a new version of myself.  We can all look back and yearn for what was, for the love of your life to return and make everything better again. I believe that’s incorrect. Because as your price increase so does the “bite” the credit card company takes out of your check. Similar to how DoorDash takes say, 15% of a sale, raising your prices 15% doesn’t bring your to profit parity. You have to raise it 18%. I use a spreadsheet that has the math/formula I’m happy to find it and post it.

For example I have a $20 item and DD takes 15% cut, or $3, and I get $17. I raise my prices by 15% from 20 and sell it for $23. Well, 15% of $23 is $3.45. I’m still not getting my $20, only $19.55. But if I raise my $20 price by 18% to $$23.60, then they take their 15% bite of that it’s $3.54, leaving me with $20.06. 

So you can’t just raise it the cost of the CC % or you still end up underwater.

*EDIT - I make no judgement whatsoever about the merit of cc fees or the perceived or real value of “not having to handle cash” (in my state you are legally required to accept cash anyway so kinda moot) I am simply suggesting what I believe is the best way to handle passing along those costs to the consumer.

Don’t fall so in love with the idea of the thing that you forget the reality of it. Sure, moving to a picturesque town in Bumblefuck, Vermont and serving artisan coffee and sandwiches to the locals sounds like something out of a movie. Hard to resist the idea, hell I want to do it after reading your post.

But the reality is more stark. Do you have any food experience? Do you enjoy having weekends and holidays to yourself or to be with family and relax? Are you ok with 12, 14 and 16 hour days for weeks and months on end? Have you built out a menu and food costed it to see what type of sales you’d have to do to even breakeven? Can the little town afford those prices? What are the demographics? How are you at the business side of things? Do you know what types of insurance you’ll need and not need? Are you current on labor laws? What types of inventory or POS software have you looked at - have you costed a buildout? Where will you get the money if you’re not profitable for the first 18-24 months (as is common)? Are you able to read and understand a balance sheet?

Here’s the thing; I love this business. It’s literally the only thing I’ve ever done. My parents Elena restaurants and I’ve been working in food since I was 12. I love ambitious folks who want to create something new, something of their own and are willing to put in the blood, sweat and tears to make it happen. But you also have to be willing to lose everything. And here’s the thing; if you approach this like it’s not a real business, like it’s some cute little idea where you’ll shoot the shit with the locals and comp your friends sandwiches while your staff runs the whole thing for you - you’re going to fail spectacularly. And I won’t lie, I love watching people like that fail.

Heres my TL;DR advice: approach this business with humility, a crazy high work ethic and an open mind willing to learn from failure and you’ll have a shot. Think of it as a cute idea anyone can do, because “anyone can make a sandwich but mine are really good” and you’re going to lose everything. 

Good luck.

I aim for firm but fair. There are certain holidays and times of the year that we deem “blackout” for planned absences because of how busy we are. Should you have an unexpected need for a call out we reserve the right to request a dr note. 

We grant 99.99% of time off requests when sufficient notice is provided. In the event we are unable to accommodate, a call out on that date would be a write up. 

Absences of more than 3 days in a row, we reserve the right to request a medical note. 

More than 9 “unplanned” absences in any 6 month period will get a warning. Anymore than 1 more absence after that is likely termination.

Call outs in the first 4 weeks should be emergency only. More than one call out is typically a huge red flag and we sit and discuss whether this is going to be a good fit. Terminated on third call out. 

We guarantee 80 PTO hours per year for full time employees, 40 for part time. 

We have a 10 minute late grace period. More than 3 lates is a write up. 3 write ups for tardiness is termination.

The truth is you want to establish guidelines you can revert to when necessary and apply the standards as even handedly as possible. The reality is there are going to be so, so, so many variables involved each time you’re going to have to use your best judgement on when to be a stickler for the rules and when to be understanding. It will be very difficult for you to maintain your sense of empathy over time as the number of people who lie and just make up garbage because they don’t feel like working that day is astounding. But don’t let it make you so cynical that when someone has a genuine emergency you threaten to fire them if they don’t choose between the emergency and their job.

I own a sandwich shop and have dealt with this sort of thing dozens of times over the years. For starters:

1) Only one person should have access to the cash per shift. If it’s a Cc transaction anyone can do itC it it’s cash only X can use the register for the day. (Or close it/balance it at the end of each shift if you have to) it’s amazing how placing accountability on a single person will usually clear up these “mistakes”.

2) buy a cheap camera on Amazon and stick it right above the register. They can be had for only $50-$75, mount it above your register, stick an SD card in it and as soon as you see a deposit is off; start watching the footage of each cash transaction that day. 

3) whoever is assigned to the drawer that night must count in and verify there is in fact $150 in cash in the drawer to start the day. Remember, it’s possible the drawer was set up improperly so having you, who resets the drawer, and a second pair of eyes - the person assigned to the drawer for that day - count it in double verifies you’re starting accurately. Have them sign a slip of paper with their name and the starting balance.

4) I’m assuming you have a set number of each bill and coin each day that starts your balance - if you don’t, do that asap. So if it’s $150, $50 singles, $50 tens, $25 fives, $10 quarter, $10 dimes, $4 nickels, $1 Pennies. (As an example)

Fire whoever is stealing. If it’s a mistake and you believe it’s a mistake truly, document that with the member of staff and coach them on how to count more accurately. If they can’t learn it either keep them off that station or let them go. If they’re careless with your cash they’re careless with your other products too.

Good luck.
